title: Heat into work: the first law and engines

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the work stopping at a Carnot line set by the two temperatures, while the cooling and exhaust take up the rest so all three still add back to the fuel, when you drag the work wider.
interactive.title: The engine's energy split
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens. The first pictures are a cylinder of gas under a piston, a still drawing. Heat goes in at the bottom, the piston moves, and a small pressure–volume chart shades the area under the gas's line, which is the work it does. The main picture is an engine's energy split. A band of fuel energy, 1,000 kW, flows into an engine and leaves as three flows whose widths you drag: work out, cooling water and exhaust. You drag the border between work and cooling, and the border between cooling and exhaust. The exhaust takes whatever is left, so the three always add back to 1,000 kW. That is the first law. Work opens at 35%, 350 kW, cooling at 30%, 300 kW, and exhaust at 35%, 350 kW. A shaded range marks 60 to 70% of the fuel, where a typical engine's cooling plus exhaust sits. Two sliders set the hot side's temperature, 500 to 1,500 K, opening at 800 K, and the cold side's, 270 to 350 K, opening at 300 K. A Carnot line sits across the work flow at 1 − T cold ÷ T hot of the fuel. At 800 K and 300 K that is 1 − 300 ÷ 800 = 62.5%, 625 kW. Drag the work past it and it stops at the line, in red. Lower the line below the work, and the work is pushed down with it, the difference going to the exhaust. The limit is a ratio of temperatures, so the sliders are in kelvin, counted from true zero. A generator skin relabels the work as electrical output and the cooling flow as what the cooler must carry. The three readouts wrap onto two rows on a phone. Screen by screen. 1 shows the cylinder taking in 500 J of heat while the gas, at a steady 200 kPa, pushes the piston out by 1 L, 0.001 m³. That is 200 kPa × 0.001 m³ = 200 J of work, and the internal energy rises 500 − 200 = 300 J. 2 asks: a gas takes in 400 J of heat and does 400 J of work. How much does its internal energy change? 0 J, 800 J or 400 J. 3 shows the piston locked: 500 J in, no work, internal energy up 500 J. Then the piston pushed in: work done on the gas counts as minus. 4 asks: 300 J of work pushes the piston in and the gas gives out 100 J of heat. What is the change? Up 200 J, down 400 J or down 200 J. 5 shows a loop on the pressure–volume chart. The gas pushes out while hot, is cooled, then is squeezed back while cool, at a lower pressure. So the squeeze takes less work than the push gave. The gas comes back to its start, so the work over the loop is the heat taken in minus the heat given out, and the loop's area is that work. The cooling is the heat given out. 6 asks, before the main picture: fuel brings 1,000 kW, the work is 350 kW and the cooling water carries 300 kW. What does the exhaust carry? 350 kW, 650 kW or 700 kW. 7 shows the energy split and the shaded 60 to 70% range. 8 asks: if cooling and exhaust carry 60 to 70% of 1,000 kW, how much work is left in this picture? 300 to 400 kW, 600 to 700 kW, or 1,000 kW with the heat on top. 9 shows the Carnot line, 62.5% at 800 K and 300 K, and 75% when the hot side is 1,200 K. 10 asks: a maker claims 75% from an engine with a hot side at 727 °C and a cold side at 27 °C. Possible? No, the limit is 70%; yes, the limit is about 96%; or yes, if its friction is low enough. 11 shows the generator skin, 350 kW of electrical output and a cooler carrying 300 kW. 12 and 13 mix it all. 12: a generator set gives 400 kW of electrical output from 40% of its fuel, and its cooling carries 30% of the fuel. What must the cooler carry? 300 kW, 120 kW or 600 kW. 13: seawater warming 10 °C must carry that 300 kW away. What flow? About 7.8 kg/s, about 7.1 kg/s or 30 kg/s.
interactive.ignores: The engine is shown as three flows. A real engine also sheds some heat from its hot casing into the room. The Carnot line assumes all the heat is taken in at the hot temperature and all given out at the cold one. A real diesel's gas passes through many temperatures each turn, so which two fit it is debated, and the sliders leave the choice to you. The generator skin counts all the engine's work as electrical output, though a real alternator turns a little into heat of its own. The flows are steady averages over many turns of the engine. The cylinder's gas is ideal and its piston has no friction.

explain.text:
An engine turns heat into work, but only ever part of it. Energy is not made or destroyed on the way, so every kilowatt of fuel leaves as work or as heat carried away. It starts with a gas in a cylinder under a piston. Heat the gas, and it can push the piston out, doing work. Or it can keep the energy, stored in the gas itself. That stored energy is its [[internal energy]]. The [[first law of thermodynamics]] says the rise in internal energy is the heat put in minus the work the gas does.[^1] Put 500 J of heat in while the gas does 200 J of work, and its internal energy rises by 300 J.

The work is the push times how far the piston moves. On a pressure–volume chart it is the area under the gas's line, as in Calculus fundamentals. At a steady 200 kPa, moving the piston out by 1 L, 0.001 m³, takes 200 kPa × 0.001 m³ = 200 J. Count heat into the gas as plus, and work done by the gas as plus. Lock the piston and no work is done, so all the heat stays in the gas. Push the piston in, and the work is done on the gas. That work counts as minus, so taking it off adds to the internal energy.

An engine runs its gas round a loop, back to where it started, so its internal energy comes back too. Over each loop, the work out is the heat taken in minus the heat given out. That work is the loop's area on the chart. No engine running in a loop can turn all its heat into work.[^2] One way to picture it: to go round again, the gas must be squeezed back. Squeezed while still hot, it pushes back as hard as it pushed out, and takes back all its work. Cooled first, it pushes back less, so the squeeze costs less than the push gave. That cooling is heat given out to somewhere colder.

A diesel swaps its gas every turn, but the same balance holds. In steady running nothing builds up inside it, so the energy in each second equals the energy out. The fuel's energy leaves three ways: work at the shaft, heat in the cooling water and heat in the exhaust. People often call that heat a loss, but nothing is lost. It is heat rejected, carried away, and every kilowatt can be followed. In a typical reciprocating engine, the cooling and exhaust carry 60 to 70% of the fuel's energy.[^3] Say the fuel brings 1,000 kW and the shaft gives 350 kW. Then 650 kW is rejected. If the cooling water carries 300 kW, the exhaust carries the other 350 kW. On a generator set, that 350 kW of work is the electrical output. The cooler carries 300 kW, nearly as much. So a cooler is sized on the heat the engine rejects, not on the set's rating.

How big could the work be? Textbooks add that no engine taking in heat at a hot temperature and giving it out at a cold one can beat the [[Carnot limit]], 1 − T cold ÷ T hot. With a hot side at 800 K and a cold side at 300 K, that is 1 − 300 ÷ 800 = 62.5%. It is a ratio of temperatures, and a ratio needs true zero, as you saw with gases. So both go in kelvin. Done in Celsius, the same sum gives about 95%, which is nonsense. Only the two temperatures move the limit. A hotter hot side or a colder cold side raises it. Less friction or a bigger engine cannot. How the limit applies to a real diesel is debated. A diesel burns its fuel inside the cylinder, so it is not quite the engine the limit describes. Some engineers say the limit does not bind a diesel at all. Others take the flame and the surroundings as the two temperatures and still treat it as a cap. The answer turns on which two temperatures you choose. Large marine two-stroke diesels reject about half of their fuel energy as heat.[^4]

**Every kilowatt of fuel leaves an engine as work, cooling or exhaust, and an engine running in a loop cannot turn all of it into work.[^2]**

analogy.text: Think of a motor's power balance. The supply feeds in electrical power. The shaft gives out mechanical power, and the rest leaves as heat in the windings and the core. Add the shaft power to the heat and you get the input, every time. An engine's fuel, work, cooling and exhaust balance the same way.
analogy.breaks: Nothing in physics stops a motor getting ever closer to turning all its input into work. Its losses are a matter of design. A heat engine is capped by its two temperatures before any design starts, so some heat must always leave it.

practice.text:
**An energy balance on an engine or a generator set**
- Start from the fuel energy, in kW.
- Take off the work. On a generator set, that is the electrical output.
- Split the rest between the cooling and the exhaust.
- Check the flows add back to the fuel.
- Check the work's share sits under the Carnot limit, with both temperatures in kelvin.

**Rules of thumb:** In a typical reciprocating engine, cooling and exhaust carry 60 to 70% of the fuel energy.[^3] A cooler is sized on the heat the engine rejects to its cooling water, not on the set's rating.

**Worked example:** A generator set gives 400 kW of electrical output at 40% efficiency, fuel to electrical output. So the fuel brings 400 ÷ 0.4 = 1,000 kW, and 600 kW is rejected. Say the cooling takes 30% of the fuel, 300 kW. Each kilogram of seawater warming 10 °C carries 3,850 × 10 = 38,500 J. So the cooler needs 300,000 ÷ 38,500, about 7.8 kg/s of seawater.

**Common mistakes**
- Getting the sign of work wrong. Work done by the gas is taken off the heat. Work done on it is added.
- Treating heat rejected as gone. It all goes somewhere, and the cooler has to carry its share.
- Putting Celsius into the Carnot limit. Use kelvin.
- Thinking better engineering lifts the Carnot limit. Only the temperatures move it.
- Multiplying by the efficiency to find the fuel. Divide the output by it.

sources.title: First Law of Thermodynamics
sources.quote: The first law of thermodynamics defines the internal energy (E) as equal to the difference of the heat transfer (Q) into a system and the work (W) done by the system.

views.label: Some engine engineers
views.text: A diesel burns its fuel inside the cylinder and swaps its gas every cycle, so it is not a Carnot engine. The Carnot limit is not its real limit, and treating it as one is a mistake.

views.label: Others, including marine engine researchers
views.text: Choose the flame's temperature as the hot side and the surroundings as the cold side, and the Carnot limit still caps any engine. The best large marine diesels can be judged against it.
